newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria army rulers pledge to end fuel crisis soon.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria army rulers pledge to end fuel crisis soon.

text.p: Nigeria's military rulers, after emergency talks in the capital Abuja, pledged on Monday to end within two days a five-week-old fuel shortage that has gripped Africa's leading oil-producing nation.
"The commander-in-chief (military ruler General Sani Abacha) has directed that fuel should be made available," the military administrator of northern Kano state told reporters after the talks.
"There will be enough fuel in the country within 48 hours," Colonel Dominic Oneya said.

He did not say how this will be done but it was the most categorical response by the military government to the crisis which has forced hundreds of thousands of commuters to trek to work and shut many businesses.

The few buses available have increased fares three-fold in Lagos, the six-million-strong commercial hub, which has forced many low-paid government workers who are unable to afford such high fares to stay at home.
In Lagos, few pump stations are still dispensing fuel while rows and rows of immobilised vehicles have become a familiar feature of the city.

A black market for the precious commodity is thriving. Touts charge five to 10 times the official pump price but motorists are finding they risk buying adulterated fuel in addition to paying high prices.
Reports across Nigeria painted similar pictures of severe hardship being encountered by Nigerians as a result of the fuel crunch.
Abacha held a series of top-level meetings in the capital Abuja on Monday culminating in the national council of state which groups military administrators of all 36 states.
Officials said the security implication of the crisis was exhaustively discussed by the council.
Nigeria pumps roughly two million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil and exports all except for 250,000 bpd allocated to its four local refineries for processing into fuel products.

No exact reason for the current fuel crunch has been officially stated but the refineries have long been operating at less than a fraction of their 445,000 bpd nameplate capacity because of lack of maintenance.
The populous African nation has frequently experienced fuel shortages but the current one is the most serious.

Uzor Okeke, director-general of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria warned last week of an imminent collapse of industries if the situation did not improve soon, labelling the crisis "a national shame."

Opposition newspapers said a peaceful demonstration was staged in Kano, Abacha's home state, on Monday to demand an immediate normalisation of the situation while university students had also warned of public protests if the situation was not redressed.

With Africa's most populous nation of 104 million dependent on road transport, the crisis is already translating into higher food prices as traders bringing in farm produce from rural areas face transport difficulties.
"We go to the interior to buy food items but we can't find transport to bring them in," said Chika Nwosu, a Lagos grocer, adding that harvests were already being lost to the fuel crisis.
